decks.title: Bank Reconciliation Statement — Part 1: Causes of Difference and Preparing the Statement
goals: Explain why the cash book and the pass book show different balances, and name the timing differences, bank items and errors
Prepare a reconciliation statement from a favourable balance or an overdraft in either book
Use the plus and minus (two-column) form as an alternative

slides.heading: The bank reconciliation statement
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **why the two books differ**, the **causes**, and how to **prepare the statement** from a favourable balance or an overdraft.

nodes.label: Check it against the other balance

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the firm compares its cash book with the pass book, finds every difference, prepares the statement and checks that it reaches the balance of the other book
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to bank reconciliation. A firm with a bank account keeps a cash book, and the bank sends a pass book. At any date their balances usually differ. In this part we find out why, sort the causes of difference, and prepare the statement that explains it, from either book and for a favourable balance or an overdraft.

slides.heading: Two records of one account
slides.body_md: The **cash book** is the firm's own record of its bank account; the **pass book** is the bank's record of the same account.

rows: The firm's dealings with the bank, written by the firm
The firm's account as the bank records it
The firm deposits or issues a cheque
The bank credits, pays or acts on its own

visual.alt: Table comparing the cash book bank column and the pass book on who keeps each, what each shows, which side is a favourable balance, which side is an overdraft and when entries are made
visual.caption: Two records of one account

slides.narration: The same bank account is written down twice. The firm writes it in the bank column of its cash book. The bank writes it in the pass book, also called the bank statement. A favourable balance is a debit balance in the cash book but a credit balance in the pass book, because the bank looks at the account from its own side.

slides.heading: The pass book is the mirror image
slides.body_md: What is a **debit** in the cash book is a **credit** in the pass book, and the other way round.

rows: A cheque is deposited and collected
A cheque issued by the firm is paid
Credit, once the firm writes them
Debit, once the firm writes it

visual.alt: Table of the mirror image: a receipt is a debit in the cash book and a credit in the pass book, a payment is a credit in the cash book and a debit in the pass book, and a favourable balance is a debit balance in the cash book and a credit balance in the pass book
visual.caption: The pass book is the mirror image of the cash book

slides.narration: When the firm deposits a cheque, it debits the bank column. The bank credits the firm. When the firm pays by cheque, it credits the bank column, and the bank debits the firm. Bank charges and interest follow the same mirror pattern. So if every entry were made on the same day in both books, the two balances would always agree.

slides.heading: Why prepare the statement
slides.body_md: A **bank reconciliation statement** shows how the balance of the cash book and the balance of the pass book are related on a given date.

rows: An entry made twice, left out or on the wrong side shows up as a difference
Charges, interest and direct payments are brought to the firm's notice
The balance the firm can really draw on is made clear
A cheque that stays unpresented for long is noticed
The auditor and the lender can see that the balances are explained

visual.alt: Table of five purposes of a bank reconciliation statement: finding errors, finding unrecorded bank items, knowing the true bank balance, checking on delay and fraud, and supporting the accounts

slides.narration: The statement has five uses. It finds errors, because an entry made twice or left out shows as a difference. It brings unrecorded bank items to notice. It tells the firm its true bank balance. It shows delays and possible fraud. And it supports the accounts for the auditor and the lender.

slides.heading: Quick check: the purpose
slides.body_md: Recall what the statement does for the firm.
slides.narration: Think about what the statement lists and what it leaves unchanged. Does it alter the books, or does it explain the difference between them?

slides.heading: Timing differences
slides.body_md: A **timing difference** arises because both books record the same transaction, but on different dates. It corrects itself, so the cash book needs no entry.

headers: Pass book balance compared with cash book balance
rows: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment
Cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank

visual.alt: Table of the two timing differences: cheques issued but not yet presented, which make the pass book balance higher, and cheques deposited but not yet credited, which make it lower; both are recorded first in the cash book
visual.caption: Timing differences correct themselves

slides.narration: Two timing differences are common. A cheque issued by the firm is entered at once in the cash book, but the bank pays it only when the supplier presents it. And a cheque deposited by the firm is entered at once, but the bank credits it only after collection. At the month end such cheques sit in one book alone.

slides.heading: Items known first from the pass book
slides.body_md: The bank also acts **on its own** or on standing instructions. The firm learns of these items only from the pass book, so the cash book **needs an entry** for each.

headers: Item known first from the pass book
Pass book balance compared with cash book balance
Entry needed in the cash book
rows: Bank charges debited by the bank
Interest on overdraft debited by the bank
Direct deposit by a customer into the bank
Payment made by the bank on standing instruction
Dividend or rent collected by the bank

visual.alt: Table of items first recorded by the bank: bank charges, interest on overdraft, interest credited, direct deposits, payments on standing instruction, amounts collected and cheques returned unpaid, with the effect on the pass book and the entry the cash book must make
visual.caption: Bank items need an entry in the cash book

slides.narration: The bank charges for its services, charges interest on an overdraft, credits interest on a balance, collects dividends or rent, pays instalments on standing instruction, receives direct deposits, and returns unpaid cheques. All of these appear first in the pass book. The firm must enter them in its cash book when it learns of them.

slides.heading: Errors in either book
slides.body_md: A wrong entry in either book also makes the balances differ. An error stays until it is **corrected**, by the firm if it is in the cash book and by the bank if it is in the pass book.

rows: A receipt entered twice in the cash book
A payment left out of the cash book
A cheque entered on the wrong side of the cash book
Cash book out by twice the amount
The bank credits another customer's deposit to the firm
The bank debits a cheque twice

visual.alt: Table of five errors: a receipt entered twice, a payment left out and a cheque on the wrong side are errors of the cash book corrected by the firm, while the bank crediting another customer or debiting a cheque twice are errors of the pass book corrected by the bank
visual.caption: Errors can lie in either book

slides.narration: Errors can lie in either book. The firm may enter a receipt twice, leave out a payment, or write a cheque on the wrong side. A cheque on the wrong side makes the balance wrong by twice the amount. The bank may also make a mistake, and then the bank must correct it. A reconciliation brings such errors to light.

slides.heading: Quick check: a cheque not yet paid
slides.body_md: Decide which kind of difference this is.
slides.narration: The firm has already recorded the payment. Ask whether the bank has paid it yet, and which of the listed causes fits that situation.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sorting the differences
slides.body_md: **Meera Spinners**, an imagined firm, lists six differences at the month end. Sort each into a timing difference, a bank item or an error, and say which book records it first.
bullets: Timing differences need no cash book entry.
Bank items and errors of the cash book **do** need one.

headers: Item found by Meera Spinners, an imagined firm
Entry needed in the cash book?
rows: A cheque deposited on the last day, credited next month
Interest credited by the bank on the last day
A receipt entered twice in the cash book
A cheque issued, paid by the bank next month
Bank charges debited on the last day

visual.alt: Table sorting six items found by Meera Spinners into timing differences, bank items and an error, with the book that records each first and whether the cash book needs an entry
visual.caption: Sorting the differences

slides.narration: Meera Spinners lists six items. A cheque deposited on the last day and credited next month is a timing difference, in the cash book first. Interest credited, bank charges and a cheque returned unpaid are bank items, in the pass book first. A receipt entered twice is an error of the cash book. A cheque issued and paid next month is a timing difference.

slides.heading: Effect of each cause on the two balances
slides.body_md: To reconcile, ask of every item: does it make the pass book balance **higher** or **lower** than the cash book balance?

rows: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment
Cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank
Bank charges debited by the bank
Interest on overdraft debited by the bank
Direct deposit by a customer into the bank
Payment made by the bank on standing instruction
Dividend or rent collected by the bank

visual.alt: Table of the effect of each cause of difference on the pass book balance compared with the cash book balance, generated from the nine causes
visual.caption: Which book is higher because of each cause

slides.narration: This table gives the effect of each cause on the pass book compared with the cash book. A cheque issued but not presented makes the pass book higher, because the bank has not paid it. A deposit not credited makes the pass book lower. Charges, a payment by the bank and a returned cheque make it lower. Interest, direct deposits and collections make it higher.

slides.heading: Starting from the cash book
slides.body_md: To reach the pass book balance, **add** the items that make the pass book higher and **deduct** those that make it lower.

rows: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment
Cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank
Bank charges debited by the bank
Interest on overdraft debited by the bank
Direct deposit by a customer into the bank
Payment made by the bank on standing instruction
Dividend or rent collected by the bank

visual.alt: Table of the nine causes of difference with the book that records each first and whether the item is added or deducted when the statement starts from a favourable cash book balance
visual.caption: Starting from the cash book

slides.narration: When the statement starts from the cash book, each item is applied as it stands. Items that make the pass book higher are added, such as cheques issued but not presented, interest and direct deposits. Items that make it lower are deducted, such as deposits not credited, charges and returned cheques. The result is the pass book balance.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from the cash book
slides.body_md: **Vasudha Pottery Works**, an imagined firm, has ₹48,600 in its cash book on 31 March 2028. Six differences are found. The result is the pass book balance of ₹56,910.
bullets: Cheques issued but not presented and the bank's credits are **added**.
Deposits not credited, charges and the returned cheque are **deducted**.

rows: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment
Direct deposit by a customer, Pranav Iyer
Cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank
Bank charges debited by the bank
Cheque of Zubair Stores returned unpaid

visual.alt: Bank reconciliation statement of Vasudha Pottery Works, an imagined firm, as on 31 March 2028, starting from the cash book balance of forty eight thousand six hundred rupees with six items and reaching the pass book balance of fifty six thousand nine hundred ten rupees
visual.caption: Vasudha Pottery Works, 31 March 2028

slides.narration: Vasudha Pottery Works has rupees forty eight thousand six hundred in the cash book. Cheques issued, interest and a direct deposit are added. Deposits not credited, bank charges and a cheque returned unpaid are deducted. The statement ends at rupees fifty six thousand nine hundred ten, which agrees with the pass book. Always finish by comparing with the other book.

slides.heading: Starting from the pass book
slides.body_md: Starting from the pass book **reverses every treatment**, because the items now move the balance the other way.

rows: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment
Cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank
Bank charges debited by the bank
Interest on overdraft debited by the bank
Direct deposit by a customer into the bank
Payment made by the bank on standing instruction
Dividend or rent collected by the bank

visual.alt: Table of the nine causes of difference with the book that records each first and whether the item is added or deducted when the statement starts from a favourable pass book balance: every treatment is the reverse of the cash book start
visual.caption: Starting from the pass book

slides.narration: When the statement starts from the pass book, each treatment is reversed. A cheque issued but not presented is deducted, because the pass book is higher than the cash book by that amount. A deposit not credited is added. Charges and returned cheques are added back, and interest and direct deposits are deducted. The result is the cash book balance.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: an overdraft as per the pass book
slides.body_md: **Jasmeet Dye House**, an imagined firm, has an overdraft of ₹26,400 as per its pass book on 30 June 2028. Four items are found. The overdraft as per the cash book is ₹17,950.
bullets: Items that **deepen** the overdraft are added.
Items that **reduce** it are deducted.

rows: Cheques issued but not yet presented
Cheques deposited but not yet credited
Interest on overdraft debited by the bank
Insurance premium paid by the bank on standing instruction

visual.alt: Statement of Jasmeet Dye House, an imagined firm, as on 30 June 2028, starting from an overdraft of twenty six thousand four hundred rupees as per the pass book and reaching an overdraft of seventeen thousand nine hundred fifty rupees as per the cash book
visual.caption: Jasmeet Dye House: from an overdraft as per the pass book

slides.narration: Jasmeet Dye House starts from an overdraft of rupees twenty six thousand four hundred in the pass book. Cheques issued but not presented are added, because they make the overdraft in the cash book the deeper one. Deposits not credited, interest on overdraft and the standing instruction payment are deducted. The statement shows an overdraft of rupees seventeen thousand nine hundred fifty in the cash book.

slides.heading: Quick check: the first step
slides.body_md: Apply the rule for the cash book start.
slides.narration: Remember the rule for a statement that starts from the cash book. Ask whether the bank has paid the cheque, and whether the pass book is therefore higher or lower than the cash book.

slides.heading: All four starting points
slides.body_md: The firm can start from the **cash book or the pass book**, with a **favourable balance or an overdraft**. The one grid covers all four.

rows: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment
Cheques deposited but not yet credited by the bank
Bank charges debited by the bank
Interest on overdraft debited by the bank
Direct deposit by a customer into the bank
Payment made by the bank on standing instruction
Dividend or rent collected by the bank

visual.alt: Table of the nine causes of difference with Add or Less for each of the four starting points: a favourable or an overdraft balance of the cash book, and a favourable or an overdraft balance of the pass book
visual.caption: All four starting points

slides.narration: This grid shows the treatment of every cause for all four starting points. When you start from an overdraft, the add and less groups swap, because an item that would lower a favourable balance now deepens the overdraft and is added. You can derive any cell from the cash book rule, so there is no need to memorise the whole grid.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: an overdraft as per the cash book
slides.body_md: **Ravine Textiles**, an imagined firm, has an overdraft of ₹12,300 as per its cash book on 31 October 2027. Five items are found. The overdraft as per the pass book is ₹12,100.
bullets: The deposit not credited and the bank's debits **deepen** the overdraft: add.
Cheques issued but not presented and the direct deposit **reduce** it: deduct.

rows: Cheque deposited but not yet credited
Bank charges debited by the bank
Interest on overdraft debited by the bank
Cheques issued but not yet presented

visual.alt: Statement of Ravine Textiles, an imagined firm, as on 31 October 2027, starting from an overdraft of twelve thousand three hundred rupees as per the cash book and reaching an overdraft of twelve thousand one hundred rupees as per the pass book
visual.caption: Ravine Textiles: from an overdraft as per the cash book

slides.narration: Ravine Textiles has an overdraft of rupees twelve thousand three hundred in the cash book. A deposit not yet credited, bank charges and interest on overdraft deepen the bank overdraft, so they are added. Cheques issued but not presented and a direct deposit reduce it, so they are deducted. The pass book shows an overdraft of rupees twelve thousand one hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: the two-column form
slides.body_md: The **two-column form** writes each item in a **plus** or a **minus** column. **Hemant Sports Goods**, an imagined firm, starts from its pass book of ₹63,850 and reaches the cash book balance of ₹53,230.
bullets: Plus: items that raise the balance. Minus: items that lower it.
Balance = plus total less minus total.

rows: Cheques issued but not yet presented
Cheques deposited but not yet credited
Rent collected by the bank on behalf of the firm
**Balance as per cash book (plus total less minus total)**

visual.alt: Two-column statement of Hemant Sports Goods, an imagined firm, as on 31 January 2028, starting from the pass book balance of sixty three thousand eight hundred fifty rupees in the plus column and reaching the cash book balance of fifty three thousand two hundred thirty rupees
visual.caption: Hemant Sports Goods: plus and minus columns

slides.narration: Hemant Sports Goods starts from rupees sixty three thousand eight hundred fifty in the pass book. Every item is placed in the plus column if it raises the balance and in the minus column if it lowers it. The two columns are totalled and the minus total is taken from the plus total. The result is rupees fifty three thousand two hundred thirty, the balance in the cash book.

slides.heading: Slips to avoid

rows: Adding a cheque deposited but not credited, starting from the cash book
It is already in the cash book, so the pass book is lower
Using the cash book rules when starting from the pass book
Starting from the other book reverses every treatment
Deducting an item that deepens an overdraft, as in the favourable layout
From an overdraft, an item that would lower a favourable balance makes the overdraft larger
Leaving out the heading or the date
The statement is prepared as on a date
Write: Bank reconciliation statement as on the date
The result must equal the other book's balance
Compare it with the other book

visual.alt: Table of five common slips in a reconciliation statement and the correct practice

slides.narration: Five slips cost marks. Do not add a deposit that is not credited when starting from the cash book. Do not use the cash book rules when starting from the pass book. Do not forget that an item which lowers a favourable balance is added to an overdraft. Write the heading with the date. And always check the final figure against the other book.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Two records of one account differ; the statement explains the difference
Timing differences, bank items and errors
Add cheques issued not presented; deduct deposits not credited
An item that lowers a favourable balance is added to the overdraft
Plus raises the balance, minus lowers it; total and subtract

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: need, causes, starting from the cash book, starting from the pass book, overdraft and the two-column form

slides.narration: To sum up. Two records of one bank account differ because of timing differences, bank items and errors. Starting from the cash book, add what makes the pass book higher and deduct what makes it lower. Starting from the pass book, reverse everything. From an overdraft, items that deepen it are added. The two column form uses plus and minus columns.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **heading** and the **date**, then the starting balance.
Decide first whether the balance given is **favourable or an overdraft**, and whether it is from the cash book or the pass book.
Group the items into **Add** and **Less** and give a **subtotal** for each.
End with the balance of the **other book** and check it.
GST is not examined: bank items here carry no tax working.
slides.narration: Examiners give marks for the heading, the starting balance, each group of items with its total, and the final balance. Common slips are applying the wrong rule when the starting book changes, forgetting the overdraft layout, and not checking the result against the other book.

decks.title: Bank Reconciliation Statement — Part 2: Extracts and the Amended Cash Book
goals: Match the entries of a cash book extract and a pass book extract, and identify the unmatched items, including items of the previous period
Prepare the statement from the extracts, including a case where both books show overdrafts
Prepare an amended cash book for items not yet recorded, and then the statement from its balance

slides.heading: Extracts and the amended cash book
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **matching two extracts**, items of the **previous period**, and the **amended cash book** followed by the statement.

nodes.label: Check it against the other balance

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: read the two closing balances, match the entries, list the unmatched ones, prepare the statement and check it, then correct the cash book first when needed
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In an examination the two books often come as extracts, and the balances must be found and matched before the statement can be written. In this part we match two extracts, deal with cheques left over from the previous month, handle overdrafts, and then amend the cash book first and reconcile its corrected balance.

slides.heading: The cash book extract
slides.body_md: The firm's own record. Read the **closing balance** from it. Lotus Bindery, an imagined firm, is used throughout this part.

visual.alt: Cash book bank column of Lotus Bindery, an imagined firm, for March 2028: opening balance of twenty four thousand eight hundred rupees, receipts and payments, closing balance of twenty six thousand six hundred rupees carried down
visual.caption: Lotus Bindery: cash book extract, March 2028

slides.narration: This is the bank column of the cash book of Lotus Bindery for March. It opens at rupees twenty four thousand eight hundred and closes at rupees twenty six thousand six hundred. Receipts are on the debit side and payments on the credit side. Notice the dates, because the same transaction may have a different date in the pass book.

slides.heading: The pass book extract
slides.body_md: The bank's record. It opens at the balance of the previous month and shows a **running balance**. A credit balance is a favourable one.

visual.alt: Pass book of Lotus Bindery for March 2028 with withdrawals, deposits and a running credit balance, opening at twenty seven thousand five hundred rupees and closing at twenty nine thousand thirty rupees
visual.caption: Lotus Bindery: pass book extract, March 2028

slides.narration: This is the pass book of Lotus Bindery for March. It opens at rupees twenty seven thousand five hundred, which is different from the cash book opening because of items of February. It closes at rupees twenty nine thousand thirty. Withdrawals reduce the credit balance and deposits increase it.

slides.heading: Matching the entries
slides.body_md: Tick each cash book entry against the pass book by **amount and nature**, not by date. Whatever is **left unticked** is a reconciling item.

rows: Entered in the cash book last period: now in the pass book
Entered in the cash book last period: now in the pass book

visual.alt: Table matching every transaction of Lotus Bindery in the two extracts: entries in both books, entries of the previous month now in the pass book, entries in the cash book only and entries in the pass book only
visual.caption: Matching the entries

slides.narration: Match entry with entry by amount and nature. A cheque received on the second of the month and credited on the third is matched, although the dates differ. Two cheques of the previous month appear in the pass book only, because the firm entered them last month. The unticked entries are the items of the statement.

slides.heading: Quick check: an entry on one side only
slides.body_md: Decide what an unmatched payment in the cash book means.
slides.narration: A payment is on the credit side of the cash book. If the pass book shows no matching withdrawal, ask whether the bank has paid it yet.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the statement from the extracts
slides.body_md: The statement of **Lotus Bindery** as on 31 March 2028 starts from the cash book balance of ₹26,600 and reaches the pass book balance of ₹29,030.
bullets: Three unmatched items raise the balance and three lower it.
The result agrees with the closing balance of the pass book extract.

rows: Cheque 3314 issued on 18 March, not yet presented
Insurance premium paid by the bank
Cheque of Pillai Brothers deposited on 29 March, credited in April

visual.alt: Statement of Lotus Bindery as on 31 March 2028 from the cash book balance of twenty six thousand six hundred rupees to the pass book balance of twenty nine thousand thirty rupees, with three items added and three deducted
visual.caption: Lotus Bindery: statement as on 31 March 2028

slides.narration: Lotus Bindery starts from rupees twenty six thousand six hundred in the cash book. A cheque issued and not presented, a direct deposit and interest are added. A cheque deposited and not credited, an insurance premium paid by the bank and bank charges are deducted. The balance is rupees twenty nine thousand thirty, which agrees with the pass book extract.

slides.heading: Items of the previous period
slides.body_md: At the start of the month the books differed by the **items of the earlier statement**. Those that clear during the month drop out; those still open stay in.

rows: Cheque no. 3305 issued in February, not yet presented
Cheque deposited in February, not yet credited

visual.alt: Opening statement of Lotus Bindery as on 1 March 2028: cash book balance of twenty four thousand eight hundred rupees, one cheque issued in February not yet presented and added, one deposit of February not yet credited and deducted, reaching the pass book balance of twenty seven thousand five hundred rupees
visual.caption: The items of the previous month

slides.narration: On the first of March the cash book showed rupees twenty four thousand eight hundred and the pass book rupees twenty seven thousand five hundred. The difference was a cheque issued in February and not yet presented, less a cheque deposited in February and not yet credited. Both were cleared in March, as the matching table showed, so neither is in the March statement.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a cheque of the earlier month still open
slides.body_md: **Saffron Linens**, an imagined firm, had cheque 6120 for ₹2,300 issued in June and not presented. It has still not been presented on 31 July 2028, so it is **listed again** with the new items. The cash book shows ₹20,100; the pass book shows ₹23,620.
bullets: The cheque of the earlier month is still a reconciling item.
A new cheque and the bank charges complete the list.

rows: Cheque 6120 issued in June, still not presented
Cheque 6127 issued on 29 July, not yet presented

visual.alt: Statement of Saffron Linens, an imagined firm, as on 31 July 2028 from the cash book balance of twenty thousand one hundred rupees to the pass book balance of twenty three thousand six hundred twenty rupees, listing cheque 6120 of June again with the new items
visual.caption: Saffron Linens: a cheque of the earlier month still open

slides.narration: Saffron Linens has rupees twenty thousand one hundred in the cash book. A cheque issued in June has still not been presented, so it stays in the statement. A new cheque issued in July is also added, and bank charges are deducted. The statement ends at rupees twenty three thousand six hundred twenty, the pass book balance. A cheque that has not cleared is never dropped.

slides.heading: Both books overdrawn
slides.body_md: Mirage Auto Parts, an imagined firm, has overdrafts in **both** books. Match as before.

rows: Entered in the cash book last period: now in the pass book

visual.alt: Table matching every transaction of Mirage Auto Parts in the two extracts, where both books show overdrafts
visual.caption: Mirage Auto Parts: matching

slides.narration: Mirage Auto Parts shows an overdraft in both books. The matching is done in the same way. One cheque of the previous month cleared in June. Two items are in the cash book only, and three are in the pass book only. Because both balances are overdrafts, take care with the layout when you write the statement.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: starting from the pass book overdraft
slides.body_md: The statement of **Mirage Auto Parts** as on 30 June 2028 starts from the pass book overdraft of ₹21,550 and reaches the cash book overdraft of ₹24,200.
bullets: The direct deposit and the cheque issued but not presented make the cash book overdraft the deeper one: they are **added**.
The deposit not credited, the interest and the charges are **deducted**.

rows: Cheque 2214 issued on 24 June, not yet presented
Cheque of Rane Garage deposited on 28 June, not yet credited

visual.alt: Statement of Mirage Auto Parts, an imagined firm, as on 30 June 2028, starting from an overdraft of twenty one thousand five hundred fifty rupees as per the pass book and reaching an overdraft of twenty four thousand two hundred rupees as per the cash book
visual.caption: Mirage Auto Parts: from an overdraft as per the pass book

slides.narration: Mirage Auto Parts starts from an overdraft of rupees twenty one thousand five hundred fifty in the pass book. The direct deposit and the cheque issued and not presented are added, because they make the overdraft in the cash book deeper. The deposit not credited, the interest and the bank charges are deducted. The result is an overdraft of rupees twenty four thousand two hundred in the cash book.

slides.heading: Why amend the cash book first
slides.body_md: Items the **bank has already acted on** and the firm has not yet written must be **entered in the cash book**. Then only the true timing differences remain.

headers: Entry in the cash book first?
rows: Payment by the bank on standing instruction
An error in the cash book
An error made by the bank

visual.alt: Table showing which items are entered in the amended cash book first and which stay in the statement: bank items and errors of the cash book are entered; cheques issued and deposited stay; an error of the bank stays
visual.caption: What goes where

slides.narration: Some questions ask first for an amended cash book. The firm enters the items that it did not know of, which are the bank items and its own errors. Cheques issued and cheques deposited are already in the cash book, so they stay in the statement. An error made by the bank is not entered by the firm.

slides.heading: Which side of the cash book
slides.body_md: An item that **raises** the bank balance is a **debit**; one that **lowers** it is a **credit**.

headers: Item entered in the amended cash book
rows: Bank charges debited by the bank
Interest on overdraft debited by the bank
Direct deposit by a customer into the bank
Payment made by the bank on standing instruction
Dividend or rent collected by the bank

sections.heading: 1. Need for a reconciliation statement
sections.body_md:
A firm with a current account keeps a **cash book** with a bank column; the bank sends a **pass book** (bank statement), its own record of the firm's account. On any date the two balances usually differ. A **bank reconciliation statement** is prepared as on a date to show how the two balances are related.

A favourable balance is a **debit** balance in the cash book and a **credit** balance in the pass book; an **overdraft** is the reverse. The pass book is the mirror image of the cash book.

**Uses:** it finds errors, shows unrecorded bank items, gives the true bank balance, exposes delay and fraud, and supports the accounts. It does not change either book.

sections.heading: 2. Causes of difference: timing differences
sections.body_md:
A **timing difference** arises when both books record the same transaction on different dates. It corrects itself, so **no cash book entry** is needed; the item is only listed in the statement.
- **Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment:** the cash book has lowered its balance; the bank has not. Pass book is **higher**.
- **Cheques deposited but not yet credited:** the cash book has raised its balance; the bank has not. Pass book is **lower**.

key_terms.definition_md: A transaction recorded by both books on different dates; it clears by itself.
A cheque the firm has credited in its cash book that the payee has not yet banked or the bank has not yet paid.

sections.heading: 3. Causes of difference: bank items and errors
sections.body_md:
The bank acts on its own or on instruction, and the firm learns of it only from the pass book: **bank charges**, **interest on overdraft**, **interest credited**, **direct deposits** by customers, **payments on standing instruction**, **dividend or rent collected** and **cheques returned unpaid** (dishonoured). The cash book needs an entry for each.

**Errors** in either book also cause a difference: in the cash book (an entry made twice, left out, on the wrong side or in a wrong amount), corrected by the firm; in the pass book, corrected by the bank. An error on the wrong side makes the balance out by **twice** the amount.

sections.heading: 4. Preparing the statement from either book
sections.body_md:
Write the heading **Bank reconciliation statement as on (date)** and start from one book.
- **From the cash book:** each item is applied by its effect on the pass book: **add** the items that make the pass book higher (cheques issued but not presented, interest, direct deposits, collections) and **deduct** those that make it lower (deposits not credited, charges, payments by the bank, dishonoured cheques). The result is the pass book balance.
- **From the pass book:** every treatment is **reversed**. The result is the cash book balance.

Always check the result against the balance of the other book.

sections.heading: 5. Overdrafts and the two-column form
sections.body_md:
**Overdraft:** when the starting balance is an overdraft, an item that would lower a favourable balance **deepens** the overdraft and is **added**; an item that would raise a favourable balance **reduces** the overdraft and is **deducted**. The result may again be an overdraft.

**Two-column (plus and minus) form:** write the starting balance (a favourable balance in the plus column, an overdraft in the minus column), then every item in the plus column if it raises the favourable balance and in the minus column if it lowers it; total both columns. The pass book or cash book balance is the **plus total less the minus total**. If the minus total is larger, the balance is an overdraft.

key_terms.definition_md: A reconciliation with a plus column and a minus column, giving the other balance as plus total less minus total.

sections.heading: 6. Preparing the statement from extracts
sections.body_md:
When the books are given as extracts:
1. Read the **closing balance** of each book (cash book bank column and pass book).
2. **Match** entries by amount and nature, not by date; matched pairs need nothing.
3. List the entries found **in one book only**.
4. Include any item of the **previous period** that is still open at the month end; an item that cleared this month falls out.
5. Prepare the statement and check that it reaches the other balance.

An entry only in the pass book is usually a bank item and needs a cash book entry (unless the bank made an error). An entry only in the cash book is usually a timing difference (unless the firm made an error).

sections.heading: 7. Amended cash book and the statement
sections.body_md:
An **amended (adjusted) cash book** brings the bank column up to date with the items the firm has not yet entered: bank charges, interest, direct deposits and payments, collections, dishonoured cheques and **corrections** of its own errors. notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are usually split (ISC Accounts)**
- 1 mark: one correct option, or the add or deduct treatment of a single item.
- 2 marks: causes of difference with reasons, or a short statement with two or three items, or a simple amended cash book of two entries.
- 3 marks: a statement of four to six items from a given balance, or a short amended cash book with the statement.
- 5 marks: a full statement from a cash book or pass book balance with six or seven items, a statement from extracts with items of the previous period, or an amended cash book followed by the statement. Marks go for the heading and date, the starting balance, each group with its subtotal, the amended cash book entries and balance, and the final balance.

**Common mistakes:** adding a deposit not credited when starting from the cash book; using the wrong rule after changing the starting book; forgetting the overdraft layout; entering cheques issued but not presented in the amended cash book; matching entries by date; listing an item of the previous period that has already cleared; not checking the result against the other book.

GST transactions are not examined.

questions.stem_md: Why does a trader who keeps a current account have to prepare a bank reconciliation statement at regular intervals?
questions.solution_md: The two balances differ; the statement explains the difference and exposes unrecorded items or errors.

answer.model_answer_md:
The cash book (bank column) and the pass book record the same account from two sides, and at a given date their balances usually differ. A reconciliation statement **finds and lists every item that causes the difference**, so that the trader can confirm that both books are right.

It also brings to light **errors, delays and bank items** the trader has not yet recorded, so that the cash book can be corrected in time.

marking_scheme.step: Two books record the same account and their balances differ
The statement lists the causes and helps to detect errors or unrecorded items

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a timing difference from an error as a cause of difference between the two books, giving one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Timing: same item, different dates. Error: wrong amount or side.

answer.model_answer_md:
- A **timing difference** arises because the two books record the same transaction on different dates, so it corrects itself later. Example: a cheque issued on 28 February and paid by the bank on 3 March.
- An **error** is a wrong entry in one of the books, which stays until it is corrected. Example: a deposit of ₹5,400 entered in the cash book as ₹4,500.

questions.stem_md: Every entry that appears in the pass book of an imagined firm but has no counterpart in its cash book is an error made by the bank.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Most such entries are genuine bank items, for example charges, interest or a direct deposit, which the firm has not yet written; only an entry the bank should not have made is a bank error.

marking_scheme.step: Correct choice (False)

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm prepares an amended cash book before its reconciliation statement. Which pair of items is entered in the cash book at that stage?

options.text_md: cheques issued but not presented and cheques deposited but not credited
cheques issued but not presented and bank charges
interest credited by the bank and bank charges debited by the bank
cheques deposited but not credited and interest credited by the bank

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** interest credited by the bank and bank charges debited by the bank. Interest and charges are known only from the pass book, so the firm writes them in the cash book. The two timing items are already in the cash book and stay in the statement; a pair that mixes a timing item with a bank item is wrong in one half.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

questions.stem_md: The bank column of the cash book of Dinesh Optics, an imagined firm, shows ₹25,000 on 31 July 2028. The pass book shows interest of ₹600 credited, charges of ₹150 debited and a customer's cheque of ₹2,000 returned unpaid, none of which is in the cash book. The balance of the amended cash book is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹23,450. The interest is a receipt and the charges and the returned cheque are payments: ₹25,000 + ₹600 − ₹150 − ₹2,000 = ₹23,450. Adding all three gives ₹27,750; deducting all three gives ₹22,250; adding the cheque and the interest and deducting the charges gives ₹27,450.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

questions.stem_md: In the amended cash book of an imagined firm, a customer's cheque of ₹3,600 that was deposited and later returned unpaid by the bank is entered

options.text_md: on the credit side of the bank column
on the debit side of the bank column
on the credit side of the cash column
only in the statement, not in the cash book

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** on the credit side of the bank column. The deposit was entered as a receipt, and the return cancels it, so the bank column is credited. Writing it on the debit side would repeat the receipt; the cash column is unconnected with the bank; and the item is a bank item that does need an entry.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (a)

questions.stem_md: A firm's pass book shows bank charges, a cheque of a customer returned unpaid, and two timing differences: a cheque issued but not presented, and a cheque deposited but not credited. After the cash book is amended, the statement from the amended cash book balance to the pass book balance contains

options.text_md: all four items
the bank charges and the dishonoured cheque only
no item, because the books then agree
the cheque issued but not presented and the cheque deposited but not credited only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the cheque issued but not presented and the cheque deposited but not credited only. The charges and the returned cheque now stand in the amended cash book, so only the two timing differences are left. The books still differ by those, so the statement is not empty, and the entered items are not repeated in it.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d)

questions.stem_md: The bank column of the cash book of Ekta Lamps, an imagined firm, shows ₹33,800 on 30 November 2028. questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After a cash book has been amended for the bank items and its own errors, the remaining difference between it and the pass book is made up of timing differences and any errors made by the bank.

**Reason (R):** The amended cash book also contains the cheques issued but not yet presented, so these are not listed in the statement.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The assertion is true: everything the firm itself failed to record has been entered. The reason is false, since the cheques issued but not presented are already in the cash book and are exactly the items that stay in the statement.

questions.stem_md: A cheque issued by an imagined firm and not yet presented for payment is entered in the amended cash book before the statement is prepared.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The cheque is already in the cash book, because the firm wrote it when it issued the cheque. It is a timing difference and appears in the statement, not as a fresh entry.

marking_scheme.step: Correct choice (False)

questions.stem_md: If the amended cash book of an imagined firm, corrected for the bank items and for its own errors, still differs from the pass book, the difference is explained by items that the firm has already entered in its cash book and by any errors in the bank's own records.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Everything that only the bank knew of has been entered. What is left is timing differences, which are in the cash book already, and errors that the bank itself must correct.

marking_scheme.step: Correct choice (True)

questions.stem_md: Why is an amended (adjusted) cash book prepared before the bank reconciliation statement, and which items are entered in it?
questions.solution_md: Bring the cash book up to date first; then list only what is still in the cash book and not in the pass book.

answer.model_answer_md:
The cash book must first record the items that the **firm itself has not yet entered** and that the bank has already acted on, so that its balance is correct and the statement contains only the true timing differences.

Items entered are: **bank charges, interest, direct deposits, direct payments, dividends collected, cheques returned unpaid** and the **correction of errors** in the cash book itself.

marking_scheme.step: Purpose: cash book brought up to date so only timing differences remain
Items entered: bank items and errors in the cash book
